query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, adherent anti‐oxidation coating (for example, an aluminide or MCrAlY layer) onto the as‐cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy will protect it against oxygen attack at high temperature while preserving its useful mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with 8–16% room-temperature ductility and 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C, but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a thin, uniform, high‐adhesion protective coating (e.g., aluminide or MCrAlY) on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure to an oxygen-containing atmosphere at elevated temperatures around 1000 °C for relevant service durations, with mechanical loading at strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, thermally stable, and adherent alumina (or similar protective oxide) scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The coating serves as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, thereby preventing the ingress of oxygen into the alloy and the formation of deleterious internal oxides, while leaving the underlying microstructure and mechanical properties essentially unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will exhibit markedly improved oxidation resistance at high temperature with minimal or no loss in tensile ductility and yield strength compared to the uncoated alloy.
generation.baseline: Uncoated HfNbTaTiZr alloy shows poor oxygen resistance despite having acceptable mechanical performance at high temperature.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective when the coating is sufficiently thin and well adhered so as not to add significant weight or introduce stress concentrations, and under temperature and strain rate conditions similar to those currently characterized (approximately 1000 °C and strain rates between 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating composition, thickness, and application process must be determined to ensure that the coating does not adversely affect the alloy’s ductility or cause spallation during thermal cycling. The performance under long-term exposure and repeated thermal/mechanical cycling is not yet known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one group with the anti-oxidation coating applied using a standardized deposition method, and one group left uncoated. Subject both groups to high-temperature oxidation tests at ~1000 °C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere for periods representative of service conditions. Subsequently, measure the mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility) at both room temperature and high temperature, and analyze the surface and cross-sectional oxidation via microscopy and spectroscopy.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, composition, and adherence (via SEM, EDS, and XRD)
High-temperature (∼1000 °C) tensile tests (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility) at strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)
Room temperature tensile tests to confirm retention of ductility
Coating integrity post thermal cycling (via adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens show no statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., similar oxide scale growth or oxygen penetration) or if their mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) are degraded relative to the uncoated specimens, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
